title: How to open an incognito window in Chrome on Mac: two ways, step by step
metaTitle: How to Open an Incognito Window in Chrome on Mac
description: How to open an incognito window in Chrome on Mac: press ⌘ Shift N, or use the three-dot menu. Steps, shortcut, and what Incognito does not hide.

intro: To open an Incognito window in Chrome on a Mac, press ⌘ Shift N. You can also click More, the three-dot icon at the top right of Chrome, and choose New Incognito window.
tldr: Press ⌘ Shift N in Chrome to open a new Incognito window straight away.
Or click More (the three-dot icon, top right) and select New Incognito window.
Check for the Incognito icon on the right side of the address bar to confirm the window is private.
Incognito deletes cookies and site data when the session ends, but websites can still see your activity.

blocks.text: Chrome gives you two routes to a new Incognito window, and both take a few seconds. The keyboard shortcut is faster if you open private windows often. The menu is better if you forget the shortcut or want to see where the option sits. Both routes open the same kind of window, so pick whichever feels natural.
Open an Incognito window with the keyboard shortcut

Make sure Chrome is the active app first. Its name should appear next to the Apple menu at the top left of your screen. Then hold Command and Shift, and tap N once. Apple writes this as Shift-Command-N, and Google's help page writes it as ⌘ + Shift + N. Both mean the same three keys.

items: ⌘ is Command, sometimes shown as Cmd.
⇧ is Shift. On most Mac keyboards it sits above the left Control key.
⌥ is Option. Chrome's Incognito shortcut does not use it.
⌃ is Control, sometimes shown as Ctrl.
N is the letter key. Press it once, with no other modifier.

blocks.text: Open Incognito from the Chrome menu

If you prefer clicking, look at the top right corner of the Chrome window. Find the three-dot icon labeled More and click it. Then select New Incognito window from the list. Google's help page describes the same steps, so you can trust the path.

rows: You open private windows several times a day
You forget the shortcut or want to be sure of the path
Close all Incognito windows, then press ⌘ Shift N
You want a fresh session with no earlier cookies

blocks.text: Check that the window is really Incognito

Normal and Incognito windows can look alike at a glance. The clearest sign is the Incognito icon on the right side of the address bar. Google's help page says a new Incognito window shows that icon there. If you do not see it, you are in a regular window.
Check the icon before you sign in to anything. Signing in to the wrong window is the easiest way to mix up your personal and private sessions.
What Incognito does and does not do

Incognito is a separate session inside Chrome. It limits what Chrome saves to your Mac while you browse. It does not sign you into your Google Account or sites. It deletes cookies and site data when the session ends, and it blocks third-party cookies by default. It also keeps bookmarks and downloads, which is easy to miss.

items: Does: limit what Chrome saves to your Mac.
Does: delete cookies and site data when the session ends.
Does: block third-party cookies by default.
Does not: hide your activity from websites, including Google sites.
Does not: hide your activity from schools, employers, or internet providers that manage the network.
Does not: stop sites that use Google services from sharing activity with Google.

blocks.text: So Incognito keeps the session off your Mac. It does not hide you from the sites you visit or the network you use. That gap is where most people get confused.

A 2017 survey of US respondents, run through Google Consumer Surveys, shows how common this confusion is. The numbers below are old, and the author notes unclear weighting, so read them as a rough snapshot.

The middle number matters most. More than half of respondents used private browsing to protect themselves from websites, which the author says is not what it is for. Treat the survey as directional, not as a measure of today's usage.
Close the Incognito window the right way

On a Mac, click Close at the top left of the Incognito window. Closing all Incognito windows ends the session. The cookies and site data from that session are deleted at that point. Your bookmarks and downloads stay where they are.
If you have two Incognito windows open, closing one leaves the other running. The session only ends when the last Incognito window closes. Close them all when you finish on a shared or borrowed Mac.
A worked example: checking a second account

Say you share a Mac with a partner, and you need to check your own email without signing them out. Open a new Incognito window with ⌘ Shift N. Sign in to your account in that window only. Your partner's sessions in the normal window are untouched.

When you finish, click Close at the top left of the window. The normal window keeps its own sign-ins, because the Incognito session is separate. Check your Downloads folder before you leave, since any files you downloaded stay on the Mac.
Fix it when the Incognito option is missing

Most of the time Incognito just opens. When it does not, the cause is usually one of two things. The shortcut may not be reaching Chrome, or your Mac is managed and an administrator has turned Incognito off. Check the simple cause first.
Click the Chrome window itself, so Chrome is the active app. Then press ⌘ Shift N again. If another app uses the same shortcut, it may catch the keys first. In that case, use the More menu instead.

blocks.title: Missing option on a work Mac
blocks.text: If IncognitoModeAvailability is set to 1, Incognito is disabled by policy. Ask whoever manages your Mac to change it, rather than hunting for a setting in Chrome.

To see the policy, open chrome://policy in a normal Chrome window. Choose Reload policies, then find IncognitoModeAvailability in the list. A value of 0 means users can open Incognito, 1 means they cannot, and 2 means they can only use Incognito. If the policy is not set, users can browse in Incognito. Restart Chrome after any policy change.
Incognito shortcut on Windows and Chrome OS

The Incognito window works the same way on other systems, but the shortcut changes. On Windows, Linux, and Chrome OS, press Ctrl + Shift + N. Google's help page lists that shortcut next to the Mac one.
Does the menu change between Chrome versions?

Google's help page for Incognito does not tie its steps to a Chrome version. Nothing on that page suggests the menu changed recently. Google's release table lists Chrome 152 with a Stable date of September 1, 2026, as its newest entry. The table does not say which version is current on Mac.
If your More menu looks different, check your Chrome version before you assume the option moved. The shortcut is the fastest test. If it works, you never need the menu.
Common mistakes with Incognito on a Mac
Most mistakes come from trusting Incognito more than it deserves. Keep these four in mind before you rely on it for anything sensitive.

items: Expecting to stay signed in. Incognito does not sign you into your Google Account or sites, so sign in again inside the window.
Leaving downloads behind. Files you download stay on your Mac. Delete any you do not want to keep.
Assuming your employer or school cannot see you. Networks they manage can still see your activity.
Leaving windows open on a shared Mac. Close every Incognito window when you finish, so the session ends.

blocks.text: Incognito does not change the network you are on. The people who run that network can still see your activity, even inside a private window.
Where to go next

Once you have closed Incognito, you may want to clear the history in your normal window. Our guide on [clearing browsing data in Chrome on a Mac](/how-to/clear-browsing-data-in-chrome) covers that. If a page is in another language, [translating a web page in Chrome](/how-to/translate-a-web-page-in-chrome) is the next thing to read.

faq.question: Does Incognito hide my browsing from my employer or school?
faq.answer: No. Incognito does not make you invisible. Schools, employers, and internet providers that manage the network may still see your activity, so treat a work or school device the same as before.

faq.question: Does Incognito save my bookmarks and downloads?
faq.answer: Yes. Incognito keeps your bookmarks and downloads. Files you download stay on your Mac after the session ends, so delete any you do not want to keep.

faq.question: What is the Incognito shortcut on a Mac?
faq.answer: Press ⌘ Shift N. Apple writes it as Shift-Command-N, and Google's help page lists the same keys. A new Incognito window opens right away.

faq.question: How do I close an Incognito window on a Mac?
faq.answer: Click Close at the top left of the window. Closing all Incognito windows ends the session and deletes the cookies and site data from it.

faq.question: Does Incognito sign me into my Google Account?
faq.answer: No. Incognito does not automatically sign you into your Google Account or sites. Sign in again inside the window if you need to.

faq.question: Does Incognito block trackers?
faq.answer: It blocks third-party cookies by default and deletes cookies and site data when the session ends. It does not stop websites from seeing your activity, so it is not a full tracking shield.

faq.question: Does the same shortcut work in installed Chrome web apps?
faq.answer: This guide did not test that. Google's help page covers the Chrome browser, not installed web apps. Try it yourself and check the window for the Incognito icon.

faq.question: What is the Incognito shortcut on Windows?
faq.answer: Press Ctrl + Shift + N on Windows, Linux, or Chrome OS. The menu path on a computer is More, then New Incognito window.

steps.name: Open Google Chrome
steps.text: Open Chrome from the Dock or from Applications. Wait for the window to appear. If Chrome is already open, click its window so it is the active app.

steps.name: Press the Incognito shortcut
steps.text: Hold Command and Shift, then tap N once. A new Incognito window opens on top of your other windows. Apple writes this as Shift-Command-N.
steps.tip: If nothing happens, click the Chrome window first and try again.

steps.name: Or open the More menu
steps.text: Look at the top right corner of the Chrome window. Click More, the three-dot icon. The Chrome menu drops down.

steps.name: Choose New Incognito window
steps.text: In the menu, select New Incognito window. Chrome opens a separate private window next to your normal ones.

steps.name: Confirm the Incognito icon
steps.text: Look at the right side of the address bar. The Incognito icon tells you this is a private window. If you do not see it, you are in a normal window.
steps.tip: Check the icon before you sign in to anything, so you know which window you are in.

steps.name: Browse, and sign in if you need to
steps.text: Incognito does not sign you into your Google Account or sites. Sign in again inside the window if you need to. Bookmarks and downloads still work as usual.

steps.name: Close the window when you finish
steps.text: Click Close at the top left of the Incognito window. Closing all Incognito windows ends the session, and cookies and site data from that session are deleted.
steps.tip: Close the window before you hand the Mac to someone else.

troubleshooting.fix: Click the Chrome window first, so Chrome is the active app, then try again. Check that you pressed Shift and N with Command, not Option. If another app uses the same shortcut, use the More menu instead.

troubleshooting.problem: The New Incognito window option is missing
troubleshooting.fix: Your Mac may be managed. Open chrome://policy in a normal window, choose Reload policies, and find IncognitoModeAvailability. Value 0 means available, 1 means disabled, and 2 means forced. Restart Chrome after any change.

troubleshooting.problem: The Incognito icon is not showing
troubleshooting.fix: You are in a regular window. Close it, then open a new Incognito window with ⌘ Shift N or the More menu. Check the right side of the address bar again.

troubleshooting.problem: A site still knows who I am in Incognito
troubleshooting.fix: That is expected. Incognito limits what Chrome saves on your Mac and blocks third-party cookies by default. Websites, including Google sites, can still see your activity, so do not rely on it to hide you from sites.

troubleshooting.problem: The More menu looks different from the steps
troubleshooting.fix: Google's help page does not tie the steps to a Chrome version. Try the shortcut first. If the menu differs, check your Chrome version against Google's release table before you assume the option moved.
